questions.title: Assessing automated applicant screening against all three providers' policies
questions.prompt:
Nuri Capital's HR team uses OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini APIs for different tasks. HR proposes:

- AI evaluates applications and ranks applicants.
- Automatically email rejection to the bottom 40% and advance higher-ranked applicants to interviews.
- Only two recruiters are available, making additional review difficult.

The AI committee must classify this as allowed, conditionally allowed, or prohibited and select controls. It must **satisfy all three policies simultaneously**, **remain compliant with Anthropic's policy effective 2026-11-12**, and **minimize recruiter workload within those limits**. Which decision and controls are most appropriate?

options.text: Conditionally allow it with qualified recruiters reviewing and able to change both advancement and rejection decisions before finalization, without separately disclosing AI use to applicants.
Conditionally allow it with human review only of rejections before sending; automate favorable interview advancements and disclose AI use in evaluation.
Conditionally allow it with qualified recruiters reviewing and able to change both advancement and rejection decisions before finalization, and disclose AI use to applicants.
Conditionally allow automatic delivery of outcomes with AI disclosure, followed by recruiter reconsideration only for applicants who appeal.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is simultaneous compliance with three policies and continued compliance under the new version. None bans AI use in hiring itself, but automated decisions without human review are not allowed. OpenAI prohibits automating high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas including employment without human review. Google prohibits unsupervised automated decisions that materially disadvantage individual rights in high-risk areas including employment. Both Anthropic's current 2025-09-15 policy and new policy classify employment as high risk, requiring qualified human review before outcomes are communicated or finalized and disclosure of AI use to affected people. The new policy additionally requires reviewers to have authority to change outcomes.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Human review is present, but both Anthropic versions require disclosure to affected people, so it fails simultaneous compliance.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The current policy has no favorable-decision review exception. The new policy's entirely favorable decision exception covers insurance payments, coverage/prior-authorization approvals, healthcare eligibility, and granting/maintaining public benefits, not employment.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Prefinalization review, authority to change outcomes, and applicant disclosure satisfy all three providers and both Anthropic versions. The two recruiters must review every decision.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Appeal-based reconsideration is retrospective and fails review before communication/finalization. Disclosure alone also does not satisfy OpenAI or Google's human-review requirements.

Additional point: The new policy explicitly says disclosure need not name Anthropic, Claude, or the model.

**References**: [OpenAI Usage Policies › Empower people](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/) · [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (September 15, 2025 version) › High-Risk Use Case Requirements](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/archive/22742366-2ef0-4c7a-a833-6523f10d3944) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective November 12, 2026) › High-risk Use Case Requirements](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)

questions.title: Clauses for a company-wide minimum standard across three providers
questions.prompt: Risk management wants one "minimum generative AI usage standard" across a company using OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google products. Include **every requirement imposed by at least one policy**, and **exclude clauses required by none**. It must also satisfy both Anthropic's current (2025-09-15) policy and the version effective 2026-11-12. Select **two clauses** to include.

options.text: Watermark all AI-generated content created by employees
For chatbots/agents conversing directly with external users, disclose that the counterpart is AI at the start of every conversation session
Do not use generative AI in legal or medical fields, even for internal drafting
Do not build systems that infer people's emotions except for medical or safety purposes
Label all externally published content "AI-generated" to comply with Google policy

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is **include anything required by any one policy** and **exclude anything required by none**. The task is to identify requirements from the strictest applicable policy and exclude excessive clauses, not to find rules shared by all three.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: None of the three policies requires users to watermark content.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Both Anthropic versions require AI disclosure for chatbots/agents conversing with external users. The current version requires it at least at each session's start; the new version permits session-start or product-interface disclosure. Session-start disclosure satisfies both. OpenAI usage policies have no such clause, but the stated principle requires including it if any provider does.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: OpenAI prohibits providing tailored advice requiring licensure without professional involvement; none prohibits internal use across the entire field.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Both Anthropic versions prohibit emotion-recognition systems except for medical/safety purposes. OpenAI prohibits emotion inference in workplace/educational settings with the same exceptions.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Google prohibits deceptively misrepresenting provenance as exclusively human-created; it does not require AI labeling on every publication.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy (2025-09-15 version) › Additional Use Case Guidelines](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/archive/22742366-2ef0-4c7a-a833-6523f10d3944) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective 2026-11-12)](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) · [OpenAI Usage Policies › Respect privacy](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/) · [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy)

questions.title: Correcting responsibility assignments using the Model Spec and Usage Policies
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Pharmaceuticals operates an OpenAI API support bot. Its policy team drafted an AI operations responsibility table, with legal-review conditions:

- [Draft 1] OpenAI's Model Spec guarantees behavior, so no internal output-review process is needed.
- [Draft 2] Cite the Model Spec as the basis for employee and user obligations.
- [Draft 3] Do not answer individualized medication questions such as dosage; refer them to a pharmacist.
- [Condition A] Only two quality staff are available; **human prereview of every response is infeasible**.
- [Condition B] Cite **documents appropriate to each responsibility**.
- [Condition C] Legal views the Model Spec as no guarantee of current behavior and requires **internal checking of actual output**.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Revise Draft 1 to require human review before every response, cite Usage Policies for Draft 2, and implement Draft 3 through developer messages.
Revise Draft 1 to provide a staffed reporting channel and periodic sample checks, cite Usage Policies for Draft 2, and implement Draft 3 through developer messages.
Provide a reporting channel and sample checks for Draft 1, retain Draft 2 because the Model Spec also sets human obligations, and implement Draft 3 through developer messages.
Retain Draft 1 but enumerate prohibited topics in developer messages and rely on Model Spec instruction-following; cite Usage Policies for Draft 2 and use developer messages for Draft 3.

questions.explanation:
Conditions A–C require mapping each draft to the correct document role. OpenAI describes the Model Spec as a public framework for intended model behavior, an aspirational target rather than a guarantee of current behavior. Product features, monitoring, and enforcement are separate safety layers outside it. Usage Policies govern how people use the API and prohibit licensed, tailored advice without qualified professional involvement, making pharmacist referral appropriate. Developers can narrow the bot's scope by changing defaults, and safety best practices recommend a human-monitored reporting channel.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Document assignments are correct, but two staff cannot prereview every response, violating Condition A.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Sampling and reporting satisfy C within A's staffing; Usage Policies govern human obligations, while developer-adjustable defaults narrow scope. Some responses may be missed compared with universal review.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Review is appropriate but document assignment violates B: Model Spec concerns model behavior, while Usage Policies govern employees and users.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Documents and scope controls are appropriate, but relying solely on compliance with an aspirational Model Spec without internal checks violates C.

**References**: [OpenAI › Our approach to the Model Spec](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-the-model-spec) · [OpenAI Usage Policies › Protect people](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/) · [OpenAI API › Safety best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.title: Assessing designs for the Claude-powered support service NuriBot
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics, the operator, is building the Claude API support service NuriBot, which customers chat with directly on the web. Legal reviews designs against Claude's Constitution and both Anthropic Usage Policy versions: current 2025-09-15 and effective 2026-11-12. Mark **Yes if the design can be adopted unchanged under both policy versions and the Constitution**, otherwise No.

1. Use a NuriBot persona and instruct it not to disclose the underlying model, while displaying 'I am NuriBot, an AI support agent' at every session start.
2. Retain that disclosure but instruct the bot to answer underlying-model questions with 'a model developed by Nuri Logistics' for brand consistency.
3. Omit on-screen disclosure and substitute Claude's default behavior of not denying it is AI when sincerely asked.
4. Limit support to shipping questions and instruct the bot to redirect off-topic questions naturally to shipping without saying it cannot help.

items.text: Use a NuriBot persona and instruct it not to disclose the underlying model, while displaying 'I am NuriBot, an AI support agent' at every session start.
Retain that disclosure but instruct the bot to answer underlying-model questions with 'a model developed by Nuri Logistics' for brand consistency.
Omit on-screen disclosure and substitute Claude's default behavior of not denying it is AI when sincerely asked.
Limit support to shipping questions and instruct the bot to redirect off-topic questions naturally to shipping without saying it cannot help.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is direct customer interaction and compliance with both policy versions plus the Constitution. The Constitution permits operators to assign different names and personas and have Claude neither confirm nor deny the underlying model by default, but not directly deny being Claude. Not denying AI status when sincerely asked, and informing users when it cannot help even if the reason cannot be given, are defaults operators cannot override. Separately, Usage Policies directly require operators to disclose AI in external-user chatbots: at least at each session start under the current policy, and at session start or in the product interface under the new one.

| Statement | Verdict | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Yes | Operators may set persona and underlying-model nondisclosure; session-start disclosure satisfies both policies. The new policy explicitly does not require naming Anthropic or Claude. |
| 2 | No | Disclosure is present, but claiming another model goes beyond neither confirming nor denying and directly denies Claude identity. |
| 3 | No | The model default acts only when asked and cannot replace the operator's disclosure duty. |
| 4 | No | Scope restriction is allowed, but hiding inability to help conflicts with a user-protection default operators cannot override. |

Additional point: When users themselves establish human-character roleplay, Claude may maintain that persona at its discretion. Users can override this default; operators cannot.

**References**: [Claude's Constitution › How to treat operators and users](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (September 15, 2025 version) › Additional Use Case Guidelines](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/archive/22742366-2ef0-4c7a-a833-6523f10d3944) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective November 12, 2026)](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)

questions.title: Provider-specific conditions for a learning assistant serving minors
questions.prompt:
Haneul Education Group plans a learning assistant for fifth graders through high-school seniors, ages 11–18, considering Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI APIs. Requirements:

- **One service must support every age in this range**.
- Student accounts contain personal information such as names and schools.
- Add controls **to the extent required by each provider's documentation**, without violating any provider condition.

Which compliance judgment is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Claude API with age verification, age-appropriate content adjustments/filtering, monitoring/reporting, and AI disclosure, plus compliance with applicable laws and public disclosure of that compliance in service policy.
Use Gemini API with the strictest safety settings, age verification, age-based filters, monitoring/reporting, AI disclosure, and parental consent for student accounts.
Use OpenAI API with age verification, age-based filters, monitoring/reporting, AI disclosure, and parental consent, processing student personal data under default data settings.
Use Claude API with age verification, age-based filters, monitoring/reporting, and AI disclosure, but admit only ages 13 and older, excluding 11–12-year-olds.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is all-age coverage, personal-data processing, and compliance with provider conditions. Gemini API terms require age 18 or older and prohibit API clients directed to or likely used by minors. Both Anthropic policy versions require organizations serving minors directly through API products to follow additional guidance covering age verification, content adjustments/filtering, monitoring/reporting, AI disclosure, applicable-law compliance, and public disclosure of compliance. OpenAI's under-18 guidance requires similar safeguards and says not to process personal data of children under 13 or the applicable digital-consent age before implementing ZDR. Choosing OpenAI therefore requires ZDR approval.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: One provider can support the whole age range with Anthropic's additional safeguards, avoiding Gemini's age restriction. Excluding OpenAI and Gemini narrows provider choice.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Age controls are present, but strict safety settings or parental consent do not override Gemini's age restriction.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Controls are present, but processing under-13 personal data before ZDR violates OpenAI's conditions.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It complies with Anthropic but excludes ages 11–12, violating full-range coverage.

Additional point: Both Anthropic and OpenAI say noncompliant organizations may receive warnings, suspension, or termination.

**References**: [Gemini API Additional Terms of Service › Age Requirements](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms) · [Claude Help Center › Responsible use of Anthropic's models: guidelines for organizations serving minors](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9307344-responsible-use-of-anthropic-s-models-guidelines-for-organizations-serving-minors) · [OpenAI API › Under 18 API Guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-checks/under-18-api-guidance) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (September 15, 2025 version) › Additional Use Case Guidelines](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/archive/22742366-2ef0-4c7a-a833-6523f10d3944)

questions.title: Meeting EEA residency requirements while retaining stored-response functionality
questions.prompt:
NuriPay's European entity wants to summarize EEA customer conversations. Its OpenAI API prototype already uses provider-stored prior responses to generate subsequent summaries. Conditions:

- [R1] Customer content must be **stored and processed within the EEA**.
- [R2] System data such as account, usage, and billing information may be processed outside the EEA under headquarters' contract.
- [R3] **Do not change the prototype's response-storage approach**.
- [R4] Compliance takes priority; additional provider approvals/contracts are acceptable, but **avoid creating internal organizations or infrastructure**.

Which configuration should be recommended?

options.text: Move to Claude API and constrain workspace storage and inference to the narrowest available regions.
Obtain OpenAI ZDR approval and a Modified Retention amendment, create a European residency project, and document that system data is outside residency coverage.
Obtain OpenAI MAM approval and a Modified Retention amendment, create a European residency project, and document that system data is outside residency coverage.
Obtain OpenAI MAM approval and create a European residency project, then create a separate European-entity organization for accounts and billing to keep system data in the EEA too.

questions.explanation:
All R1–R4 matter, with distractors failing different requirements. OpenAI European residency, covering EEA and Switzerland, stores and processes supported-endpoint customer content there. Non-US regions require MAM or ZDR approval and a Modified Retention amendment; region is selected when creating a project. Both controls exclude customer content from abuse-monitoring logs, but MAM leaves endpoint behavior unchanged while ZDR always treats response storage as off. Account, usage, and billing system data are excluded from residency, so R2 enables the design.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Claude inference offers only US or global, and workspace storage only US, so even the narrowest settings fail R1.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: R1 and R2 are met, but forced-off response storage under ZDR violates R3.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It satisfies R1–R4, at the cost of approvals/contracts and a 10% surcharge on residency endpoints for eligible models released after 2026-03-05.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: R2 already permits system data outside the EEA, so a separate organization is unnecessary and violates R4.

Additional point: Residency does not cover data passed to third parties such as remote MCP servers; adding external tools requires separate review.

**References**: [OpenAI API › Data controls in the OpenAI platform › Data residency](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) · [Claude API › Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency)

questions.title: Correcting a policy allowing personal accounts for work documents
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics discovers employees uploading work documents to personal ChatGPT Plus, personal Claude Pro, and free-tier Gemini API using personal keys in Korea. Business teams propose allowing Internal-classified material if training settings are disabled. Privacy review criteria:

- [Criterion 1] Internal material may enter only services where **nontraining is a plan/contract condition, not a personal setting**.
- [Criterion 2] Controls must be **enforceable and verifiable by company administrators**.
- [Criterion 3] Retain **at least one approved work route**.

Which policy is most appropriate?

options.text: Allow personal accounts with training settings disabled, train staff not to send ChatGPT feedback, and restrict sensitive content to Temporary Chat.
Ban all work material from generative-AI services because provider training/retention paths differ, requiring employees to summarize and translate manually.
Allow personal Gemini API keys only after employees enable billing for paid service, while prohibiting work material in personal ChatGPT and Claude accounts.
Allow work material only in company-contracted ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise, and company-billed Gemini API projects; prohibit personal accounts and keys.

questions.explanation:
Criteria 1–3 distinguish the choices. Consumer plans retain exceptions despite opt-outs: ChatGPT feedback can make a conversation eligible for training even after opt-out, and Temporary Chat may remain up to 30 days for safety. Claude consumer opt-out does not remove data from ongoing training or already trained models. Gemini unpaid submissions may be used for product improvement and human review. OpenAI business and Anthropic commercial products do not train on customer data by default, and Gemini paid services do not use prompts/responses for product improvement.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Personal settings and behavior do not satisfy Criteria 1 and 2. Training may reduce feedback/Temporary Chat risks but does not eliminate Claude consumer and Gemini free-tier paths.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: It closes training paths but leaves no approved route, violating Criterion 3.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Paid service satisfies Criterion 1, but personal keys and billing are not company-admin enforceable or verifiable, violating Criterion 2.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It costs seats and usage fees but preserves administrator-managed routes with plan-level nontraining terms.

Additional point: Feedback through rating buttons can make Anthropic commercial conversations available for training. Team/Enterprise Primary Owners and Owners can disable 'Rate chats' under Data and Privacy to close this path administratively.

**References**: [OpenAI Help › Data Controls FAQ](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/7730893-data-controls-faq) · [OpenAI › Enterprise privacy](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/) · [Claude Privacy Center › How long do you store my data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data) · [Claude Privacy Center › Is my data used for model training?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training) · [Gemini API Additional Terms of Service › Unpaid Services · Paid Services](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms)

questions.title: Gemini API data-use rules for Korean headquarters and an EEA entity
questions.prompt:
Haneul Trading's Korean headquarters and EEA entity use Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Security defines these conditions:

- [Condition 1] The EEA entity is preparing an **app for local users** and must operate it under permitted terms.
- [Condition 2] Material classified 'Minimize provider storage' must not enter **separate retention paths defined by the terms**.
- [Condition 3] Headquarters' market-research assistant must **retain Grounding with Google Search**.
- [Condition 4] Work using only public material must **not incur increased cost**.

Select **two policy provisions** satisfying all four conditions.

options.text: Operate API clients offered by the EEA entity to EEA users only as paid services.
Because Search grounding retains data for 30 days even on paid service, disable headquarters' grounding and require staff to paste search results manually.
Retain headquarters' grounding, but exclude material classified 'Minimize provider storage' from that assistant's inputs.
Because paid data terms apply to free use in the EEA, run the EEA app on the free tier to save initial launch costs.
Move even headquarters' public-material summarization to paid services in billing-enabled Cloud projects to standardize data terms.

questions.explanation:
Conditions 1–4 require combining unpaid/paid distinctions, regional exceptions, and separate grounding retention. Gemini terms require paid services when providing API clients to users in the EEA, Switzerland, and UK, while also applying paid-service data conditions to unpaid use in those regions. Google Search and Maps grounding retain prompts, contextual information, and outputs for 30 days, even on paid service, and may use them for debugging and testing.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It directly meets the paid-service requirement for EEA-user API clients and Condition 1.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: It meets Condition 2 but disabling grounding violates Condition 3; excluding classified material suffices.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It keeps classified material out of separate retention while preserving grounding.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Paid data terms do apply to free regional use, but the separate paid-only API-client requirement still applies, violating Condition 1.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: Paying for public-material work violates Condition 4. Korean unpaid submissions can be used for improvement and human review, but that is acceptable for exclusively public material.

Additional point: AI Studio linked to a billing-enabled Cloud project or Workspace enterprise account counts as paid service even when used without charge.

**References**: [Gemini API Additional Terms of Service › Use Restrictions · Unpaid Services · Paid Services](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms)

questions.title: Operational sequence for beginning PHI use in Claude Enterprise
questions.prompt:
Hangyeol Medical Foundation wants to enable HIPAA in Claude Enterprise to handle protected health information (PHI). Researchers also use Claude Code and Cowork locally and plan to enter PHI there. Security requires **assessing impact before irreversible changes**, employee notices containing **only verified actual setting changes and unavailable features**, and **PHI only in confirmed BAA-covered features**. Order these steps by documented dependencies.

- (1) The Primary Owner accepts the BAA and enables HIPAA under Organization settings > Data and privacy.
- (2) Notify employees of BAA-covered and unavailable features and begin PHI use in covered features.
- (3) Obtain the Implementation Guide and list feature-level BAA coverage and settings reset to defaults on activation.
- (4) Compare the list from (3) with actual settings to confirm resets and unavailable cloud features.
- (5) The Primary Owner applies HIPAA configuration to local Claude Code and Cowork.

items.text: The Primary Owner accepts the BAA and enables HIPAA under Organization settings > Data and privacy.
Notify employees of BAA-covered and unavailable features and begin PHI use in covered features.
Obtain the Implementation Guide and list feature-level BAA coverage and settings reset to defaults on activation.
Compare the list from (3) with actual settings to confirm resets and unavailable cloud features.
The Primary Owner applies HIPAA configuration to local Claude Code and Cowork.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is impact assessment before irreversible changes, notices based on actual results, and PHI only in BAA-covered features. Only the Primary Owner can accept the BAA and enable HIPAA; this cannot be reversed in organization settings and resets some settings. Enabling HIPAA alone does not cover local Claude Code/Cowork: the Primary Owner must separately apply their HIPAA configuration after organization activation. This irreversibly disables cloud features such as Claude Code on the web.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Review Implementation Guide | Identify impact before irreversible (1). | The guide defines feature status and activation-related changes. |
| 2 | (1) Accept BAA and enable HIPAA | Act after reviewing the impact list from (3). | Primary Owner only; irreversible. |
| 3 | (5) Configure local modes | Applies separately after organizational activation in (1). | Organization activation precedes this separate configuration. |
| 4 | (4) Verify actual settings | Both resets from (1) and cloud-feature disabling from (5) must occur first. | Cloud features are disabled when (5) is applied. |
| 5 | (2) Notify and begin PHI use | Notices use verified results from (4); research tools are not covered before (5). | PHI belongs only in BAA-covered features. |

Placing (4) immediately after (1) misses cloud features disabled by (5), violating the notice requirement.

Additional point: The Implementation Guide can be requested from Anthropic Trust Center and is also available to download and review during activation.

**References**: [Claude Help Center › HIPAA-ready Enterprise plans](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13296973-hipaa-ready-enterprise-plans)

questions.title: Translating one retention rule into three platforms' settings
questions.prompt:
Nuri Trading's sales team uses ChatGPT Enterprise, research uses Claude Enterprise, and all employees use Workspace's Gemini app. New policy:

> Retain business generative-AI conversation records for one year after last activity, then delete them, except records under legal preservation obligations.

Current state:

- Claude Enterprise retention has never been configured; researchers also use Claude Design and Claude Managed Agents.
- Legal has set the Gemini app's default Google Vault retention to indefinite and placed two litigation-related employees on hold.

Which combination **fully matches the rule while preserving legal exceptions**?

options.text: A Claude Owner sets one-year custom retention. Change Gemini's Vault default to one year and retain the two holds. Set ChatGPT administrator retention to one year.

Set Claude custom retention to one year and separately control excluded features. Change only Gemini Admin console conversation auto-deletion to one year, retaining Vault rules. Set ChatGPT to one year.
Set Claude custom retention to one year and separately control exclusions. Change Gemini Vault default to one year and remove the two holds for uniform application. Set ChatGPT to one year.

Set Claude custom retention to one year and separately control excluded features. Change Gemini Vault default to one year while preserving the two holds. Set ChatGPT administrator retention to one year.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is unconfigured Claude retention, indefinite Vault retention and holds, and legal exceptions. Each platform has different mechanisms and precedence, so the rule must map to actual controls.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Gemini, ChatGPT, and basic Claude settings are correct, but Claude Design and Managed Agents are excluded from custom retention; absent separate controls, coverage is incomplete.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Vault retention and holds override Admin console/user settings. With indefinite retention, auto-deletion only hides content from users while retaining data.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Removing holds violates legal preservation. Rule changes or deletion can immediately purge old data; Google recommends testing on a small group first.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It accounts for Claude's indefinite default and exclusions, Vault precedence and holds, and ChatGPT administrator settings. Test Vault changes on a small group first.

Additional point: Claude Enterprise custom retention has a 30-day minimum, treats a month as 30 days, and is configured by Primary Owners or Owners. Conversations flagged for policy violations follow separate rules.

**References**: [Claude Help Center › Configure custom data retention controls for Enterprise plans](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10440198) · [Google Workspace Admin › Retain Gemini app messages with Vault](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/vault/retention/retain-gemini-app-messages-with-vault) · [OpenAI › Enterprise privacy](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)

questions.title: Audit-data collection scope in a CMEK-enabled Claude Enterprise organization
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Securities uses Claude Enterprise with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). Requirements:

- **Automatically collect** audit events such as logins/settings changes and conversation content into the internal security-monitoring system.
- Developers use both Claude Code CLI and cloud sessions; policy must **openly identify audit exclusions**.
- The security operator holds the Admin role.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the Primary Owner enable and connect Compliance API; explicitly list unsupported Claude Code cloud sessions as an exclusion and control them separately.

Have an Owner manually export the latest 180 days of audit logs monthly through Data and Privacy > Export logs and upload them, deferring conversation content and cloud-session coverage to next quarter.
Have the security Admin directly open the Compliance API page, enable it, create a key, and connect monitoring, explicitly listing cloud sessions as excluded.
Have the Primary Owner enable Compliance API and omit exclusions because it covers every surface, including Claude Code cloud sessions.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is CMEK, automatic collection, and disclosed exclusions. CMEK Enterprise organizations cannot use Export logs and must obtain audit events through Compliance API. The API programmatically provides activity-feed events, conversations, files, and audit logs, and only the Primary Owner can enable it. It excludes Claude Code cloud sessions, Claude Code through Claude Platform, and sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It meets CMEK collection, role, and exclusion requirements, leaving separate cloud-session controls to design.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; applies elsewhere)**: Export logs applies without CMEK, and manual export does not meet automation.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Exclusions are disclosed, but Admins cannot view the Compliance API page or enable it; only the Primary Owner can.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Collection is correct, but claiming universal coverage hides excluded surfaces such as cloud sessions.

Additional point: For linked organizations, the parent organization's Primary Owner enables the setting, which applies across all linked organizations.

questions.title: Compensating controls after enabling connector domain restriction

Set safety metrics and minimum thresholds before testing, judge worst-case performance on an internal human-assisted dataset, repeatedly test malicious and inadvertently harmful inputs, and provide feedback channels.

questions.title: Incorporating provider-framework changes into internal model approval
questions.prompt:
Nuri Securities uses OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models and wants a provider-framework review clause for approving new frontier models and revisiting existing approvals. Conditions:

- [Condition 1] Every clause must be **supported by published provider documentation**.
- [Condition 2] Provider judgments are inputs and **do not replace internal use-case review**.
- [Condition 3] With two reviewers, trigger reviews on **publicly announced provider changes**.

Select **two clauses** meeting all conditions.

options.text: Use OpenAI's release-time system-card Preparedness results as model-specific review inputs, while conducting internal use-case review separately.
Because OpenAI deployment follows Safety Advisory Group review and leadership decisions, simplify internal risk review.
Because Google reviews safety cases before externally releasing models that reach CCLs, record released Gemini models as having reached no CCL.
When Anthropic RSP changelogs, revised Google FSF editions, or OpenAI's public requirement-adjustment announcements appear, update internal comparisons of risk areas and threshold structures.
When a competitor releases a high-risk model, assume OpenAI has lowered requirements and immediately reopen OpenAI model approvals.

- [Condition 2] Contract timelines prohibit **requests conflicting with published provider documents**.

Provide fallback models/manual work only for summaries, with bank committee reapproval when safeguards or access conditions change.

options.text: Create a dedicated Restricted workspace allowing only US inference, migrate the batch to a Claude 4.6-or-later model, and log the inference region reported in responses.
Change the existing workspace's default inference region to US, explicitly request global for marketing/internal documents to save cost, and log response inference regions.
Create a dedicated Restricted workspace allowing only US inference, retain Haiku 4.5 while specifying US on each request, and log inference regions.
Create a dedicated US-only Restricted workspace, move the batch to 4.6 or later, and simplify administration by moving marketing/internal-document jobs there too, logging all jobs together.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Model migration and 1.1-times pricing buy allowlist enforcement independent of developer mistakes and per-request region records, while other work retains global pricing.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Explicit requests override defaults and global remains allowed, failing enforcement against altered regions.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Controls and records are present, but region selection on Haiku 4.5 produces 400 errors and prevents the batch from running.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: Restricted requirements are met, but charging US pricing for unrestricted jobs violates Requirement 1's cost condition.

Seat count and nightly scheduling are distractors. Additional point: Workspaces that previously opted out of global routing automatically received US-only allowed regions and defaults.

questions.title: Designing generative-AI monitoring of employee communications
questions.prompt:
Saesol Securities must inspect employee communications under supervisory rules. Compliance proposes feeding every employee's messages and emails to generative AI to create trustworthiness scores and stress-emotion indicators identifying unusual employees. Review uses Anthropic's current 2025-09-15 policy. Constraints:

- [1] **Continuously inspect all employees' communications** to meet supervision duties.
- [2] **Comply simultaneously with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google policies**.
- [3] Three staff cannot **manually inspect every item**.
- [4] Consent is **still pending for about 30%** of employees.

Which monitoring design is most appropriate?

options.text: AI reads all consenting employees' communications and assigns trustworthiness scores, with staff reviewing high-scoring employees; use existing rule-based checks for others and omit stress indicators.

Obtain prior notice and consent through policy; AI summarizes only rule-flagged items for consenting employees, with staff making decisions. Retain rule-only checks for others and create no scores or emotion indicators.
Until consent is complete, provide notice only and let AI summarize rule-flagged communications for everyone, with three staff deciding; retain rule checks and omit scores/emotion indicators.
AI summarizes rule-flagged items for consenting employees and automatically refers employees classified as anomalous for discipline without staff confirmation; retain rule-only checks for others.

Constraints 2 and 4 are decisive. questions.title: Conditions for synthetic voices in an advertising series
questions.prompt:
Nuri Brand wants synthetic voices for three advertisements:

- (1) A reconstructed voice of the deceased founder, who consented in writing during life to advertising use; viewers may mistake it for a real recording.

- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It preserves all three concepts while separately satisfying consent and disclosure, accepting additional negotiations, reduced immersion from labels, and abandoning the actor's voice.

questions.prompt: Haneul Health reviews five practices against Google's Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy revised 2024-12-17. Apply its **deceptive-intent condition** and **educational/artistic exceptions**. Select **two prohibited practices**.

Give a fictional persona an internal-medicine-specialist title and fake license details, publishing columns intended to make readers believe a real physician advises them.
Publish a column under a physician's name after that physician reviews and revises it, disclosing AI drafting assistance.
Create a fake-specialist post labeled 'demonstration only' for internal training on fraudulent health-advertising techniques.
Distribute AI-written text with fabricated provenance claiming a professional writer wrote it personally, making readers believe it was entirely human-authored.

questions.explanation:
Deceptive intent and exceptions are decisive. Policy section 4 prohibits deceptive false claims of expertise/capability in sensitive fields—health, finance, government services, and law—under 4.3, and deceptively misrepresenting generated content as solely human-created under 4.5. It allows potential exceptions for educational, documentary, scientific, or artistic purposes, or where public benefit substantially outweighs harm.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; overinclusive)**: AI disclosure means the stated deceptive intent is absent.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Fake credentials intended to imply real medical advice constitute false expertise under 4.3.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; overinclusive)**: Physician review/revision and AI disclosure do not misrepresent expertise or provenance.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; overinclusive)**: Educational purpose and demonstration labeling avoid deception and fit the exception.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Claiming AI text is solely human-created misrepresents provenance under 4.5.

Additional point: This policy does not impose a universal AI-labeling rule; deceptive purpose is the prohibited condition.

**References**: [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy › 4. Misinformation, Misrepresentation, and Misleading Activities](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy)

questions.title: Hospital AI release scope and user notices
questions.prompt:
Haneul Hospital is developing two Gemini API features: (1) a scheduling-change chatbot and (2) explaining test results to patients and advising on medication use. Nurses currently handle questions manually and face heavy workloads. Constraints:

- [1] Follow **Gemini API Additional Terms' use restrictions and disclaimers**.
- [2] **Do not increase nurses' manual workload**.
- [3] Patient-facing notices must align with the disclaimer's purpose.

Which release scope and notice are most appropriate?

options.text: Release only (1), defer (2), and clearly state that the chatbot does not replace professional consultation.
Release both, requiring nurses to confirm every answer from (2) before delivery, with AI-assistance disclosure.
Release both, displaying 'For reference only; not professional advice' for (2), and retain answer history at the hospital.
Release both in a paid-service project, limiting (2) to explaining test values without medication-use advice.

questions.explanation:
Constraints 1 and 2 are decisive. Gemini API Additional Terms prohibit clinical-practice or medical-advice use and disclaim reliance as professional medical, legal, or financial advice. The examined wording provides no exception for clinician review, disclaimers, or paid service. Feature (2), explaining results and advising patients, should therefore be excluded from launch.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It releases the scheduling feature, defers medical interpretation, and provides an appropriate disclaimer; some patient questions remain manual.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Nurse confirmation adds workload contrary to 2, and the terms do not establish human review as an exception to the prohibited purpose.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; addresses a different situation)**: A reliance disclaimer does not authorize an otherwise prohibited use.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Paid service changes data-use terms, not use restrictions. Explaining test values still provides medical interpretation to patients.

**References**: [Gemini API Additional Terms of Service › Use Restrictions · Disclaimers](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms)

questions.title: Assigning responsibility when deploying a vendor purchasing agent
questions.prompt:
Hangyeol Solutions plans to deploy a vendor-built Claude purchasing agent unchanged. It creates/sends orders, controls browsers, and writes to ERP. Under Anthropic's policy effective 2026-11-12, the internal responsibility clause must:

- [1] Accurately assign **policy-compliance responsibility for tool, browser, and connected-system actions**.
- [2] **Require no vendor code changes**.
- [3] **Take effect immediately on deployment**.

Which clause is most appropriate?

options.text: Name the adopting department as owner, define ERP write scope and incident responsibility, request code changes adding internal approval calls at every write, and implement the policy on deployment day.
Name the adopting department as owner and define write scope and incident responsibility without code changes, but implement the policy next quarter after contract revision.

Split compliance responsibility between vendor and adopting department, define ERP write scope, let the vendor designate incident responsibility, make no code changes, and implement on deployment day.
Name the adopting department as owner, define ERP write scope and incident responsibility, make no code changes, and implement on deployment day.

questions.explanation:
Constraints 1 and 2 are decisive. Anthropic's new policy makes users responsible for ensuring agents they build or deploy comply, including actions through tools, browsers, and connected systems. Deployment makes Hangyeol responsible even though a vendor built the agent, so internal ownership, authority scope, and response responsibility should be explicit. All four clauses are operationally possible but differ in which constraint they violate.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: Responsibility is correct, but vendor code modification violates 2.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Responsibility and unchanged code are appropriate, but deferral leaves ERP writes without the policy until next quarter, violating 3.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Dividing responsibility and assigning response ownership to the vendor misstates deployer compliance responsibility under 1. Contracts may allocate costs/damages but cannot transfer that policy responsibility away from the deployer.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It defines owner, privileges, and response duties without code changes and applies immediately, satisfying all three. The adopting department bears incident-response responsibility.

questions.title: System prompts giving verified pharmacists more detailed information
questions.prompt:
A pharmaceutical-wholesale platform operator uses a Claude consultation tool and wants to provide detailed dispensing information to pharmacists verified by its licensing system. Constraints:

- [1] Detailed information goes **only to verified users**.
- [2] The **company system already determines verification**; the model does not assess licenses.
- [3] Preserve Claude's **user-protection defaults**.

Which system-prompt design is most appropriate?

options.text: Trust users' conversational claims to be pharmacists and answer in detail, limiting others to general information.
Explicitly grant company-verified users operator-level trust, limiting unverified users to general information.
Grant verified users operator-level trust but redirect requests the model cannot help with without disclosing its inability.
Grant verified users operator-level trust but ask for license numbers in conversation and have Claude judge authenticity.

questions.explanation:
Constraints 2 and 3 are decisive. Claude's Constitution permits operators to adjust/restrict defaults and grant users authority up to operator level or reduce it. It even gives an example of trusting occupational claims, but here verification authority is already assigned, so company-system results must establish trust. Operators cannot override user-protection defaults such as acknowledging inability to help.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Trusting occupational claims is allowed in principle, but self-assertion cannot replace the verification required by 1 and 2.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It leaves verification with the company, specifies permissible trust, and preserves protections. Integration work and restricting unverified pharmacists are the tradeoffs.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Hiding inability to help conflicts with a non-overridable protection, violating 3.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; addresses a different situation)**: Trust designation is appropriate, but delegating license judgment to the model violates 2; conversation cannot replace external verification.

Additional point: The Constitution is evolving, so periodically recheck cited provisions.

**References**: [Claude's Constitution › How to treat operators and users](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution)

questions.title: What developer messages may and may not change
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Software is building an OpenAI API support bot and proposes developer-message requirements:

1. Use polite language and concise formatting.
2. Politely decline topics outside product scope.
3. Answer even in areas prohibited by Usage Policies.

Review must follow the Model Spec's **chain of command and hard-rule/default distinction**, **implement permitted adjustments through developer messages without separate code**, and **reject impermissible requests while naming the source document**. Which review is most appropriate?

options.text: Implement 1/2 through developer messages and reject 3 with only 'Policy prohibits this,' naming no source.
Implement 1 through developer messages, 2 through output post-processing, and reject 3 citing Usage Policies.
Implement 1/2 through developer messages and partly allow 3 when users explicitly request it on a consent screen.
Implement 1/2 through developer messages and reject 3 citing Usage Policies.

questions.explanation:
The chain-of-command and rejection-documentation constraints are decisive. OpenAI describes hard rules as boundaries developers/users cannot override and defaults as adjustable starting points. Higher-priority instructions prevail in the OpenAI/developer/user hierarchy; tone, depth, format, and perspective can vary within safety boundaries. Model Spec addresses model behavior; Usage Policies govern how people use the service. Each proposal is operationally possible but violates different constraints.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Implementation is appropriate, but unnamed rejection evidence violates source-document requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; overengineering)**: Coding a scope restriction that developer messages can express violates the no-separate-code requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: User requests or consent cannot override hard boundaries; partial permission confuses hard rules and defaults.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It implements adjustable 1/2 through developer messages and rejects 3 with the correct source, satisfying all constraints. The requesting team still needs an explanation of the rejection.

**References**: [OpenAI › Our approach to the Model Spec](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-the-model-spec)

questions.title: Assessing statements for an internal model-behavior guide

A policy team is preparing an internal guide based on Claude's Constitution and OpenAI's Model Spec. Mark **Yes if each statement is accurate enough to use unchanged according to its source**, otherwise No.

1. Claude's Constitution describes itself as the final authority on Anthropic's vision for Claude while remaining an evolving document subject to revision.
2. OpenAI's Model Spec records models' current behavior and can prove they behave as documented.
3. Model Spec covers model behavior; Usage Policies complement it with expectations for human use of API and ChatGPT.
4. Claude's priorities—safety, ethics, instructions, helpfulness—are not rigidly lexicographic; higher values lead while lower values still inform overall judgment.

items.text: Claude's Constitution describes itself as the final authority on Anthropic's vision for Claude while remaining an evolving document subject to revision.

Model Spec covers model behavior; Usage Policies complement it with expectations for human use of API and ChatGPT.
Claude's priorities—safety, ethics, instructions, helpfulness—are not rigidly lexicographic; higher values lead while lower values still inform overall judgment.

questions.title: Permitted uses when standardizing external-affairs documents on one provider
questions.prompt:
Daon Energy's external-affairs team wants AI to draft (1) a policy-position submission lobbying a regulator, (2) a message encouraging employees' political participation that clearly identifies the company as its sender and does not target employees using personal data, and (3) explanatory materials for community residents. Apply Anthropic's current September 15, 2025 policy. Google is excluded from this quarter's security review.

The team must satisfy these constraints: (1) use one standard provider; (2) its two staff members need AI drafting for all three document types; (3) verify factual claims before submission; (4) an OpenAI contract already exists, but switching costs are acceptable; and (5) the deadline is five business days away and approximately 40 factual claims require checking. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep OpenAI, use AI only for document (3), manually draft (1) and (2), and verify all 40 claims before the deadline.
Keep OpenAI as the standard, but use a separate provider environment for (1) and (2), use OpenAI for (3), and verify all 40 claims before the deadline.
Standardize on Claude and use AI to draft all three types. Before submission, retain only verified factual claims and omit unverified ones.
Use Claude for all three types and submit by the deadline, then verify a sample of the 40 factual claims afterward.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

The decision must reconcile the single-provider and staffing requirements, as well as the tension between verification and the deadline. OpenAI expressly prohibits political campaigning and lobbying, so it cannot draft documents (1) and (2). Anthropic's applicable policy prohibits lobbying or grassroots advocacy based on false or manipulated information and mass contact with officials or voters that conceals its artificial origin; it does not list factual, transparent lobbying itself as prohibited. Google's policy prohibits deceptive false claims about democratic processes, but Google is not a candidate here. With five business days available, claims that cannot be verified should be omitted.

- {{option:A}} satisfies standardization and the provider's policy, but manually writing (1) and (2) violates the requirement that two staff members use AI drafting for all three types.
- {{option:B}} effectively uses two providers and violates the single-provider constraint.
- {{option:C}} satisfies the single-provider, AI-drafting, prior-verification, and deadline requirements. It accepts the cost of switching away from OpenAI and drops unverified claims.
- {{option:D}} meets the switching and deadline requirements, but verification after submission violates the prior-verification condition and risks lobbying based on false information.

Document (2) depends on the stated conditions that the sender is disclosed and no personal-data-based targeting occurs.

**References**: [OpenAI Usage Policies › Empower people](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/) · [Anthropic Usage Policy (September 15, 2025 version) › Lobbying, Political Campaigning](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/archive/22742366-2ef0-4c7a-a833-6523f10d3944) · [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy › 4.4](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy)

questions.title: Identifying prohibited features in a coaching app for teenagers
questions.prompt: An OpenAI API fitness and diet app serves users aged 16–17. Evaluate the following five features under the protections for minors. Judge the type of content, rather than treating age alone as the criterion. Which TWO features are prohibited?

options.text: Coaching that sharply cuts daily calorie intake to achieve quick results.
Weekly weight records displaying progress toward a goal.
Flagging age-inappropriate large weight-loss goals and advising the user to consult a parent or professional.
Evaluating body shape from a photo using derogatory comments such as 'too much flab'.
A personal challenge that gradually increases exercise time over a month and includes rest days.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:A}}, {{option:D}}**

The minors policy prohibits promoting unhealthy dieting or exercise, stigmatizing body shape or appearance, and dangerous challenges. This is a separate question from minimum-age requirements. Merely involving body weight, exercise, or a 'challenge' is not sufficient to establish a violation; the content determines the outcome.

- {{option:A}} promotes unhealthy dieting through a sharp calorie reduction and is prohibited.
- {{option:B}} records weight and progress without the stated stigma or danger, so it is not prohibited on these facts.
- {{option:C}} warns about an unsuitable goal and refers the user to help, rather than promoting it.
- {{option:D}} stigmatizes body shape and is prohibited.
- {{option:E}} increases exercise gradually and includes rest. Calling an activity a challenge does not, by itself, make it dangerous or prohibited.

**References**: [OpenAI Usage Policies › Keep minors safe](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/)

questions.title: Operational design for using Claude in collaborative-robot planning
questions.prompt:
Daon's logistics center wants Claude to plan the movement and loading operations of collaborative robots that work alongside people and apply physical force. Apply Anthropic's November 12, 2026 requirements for high-risk physical actions.

Constraints: (1) the team wants the model to calculate speed and force directly to improve throughput; (2) physical-action requirements must be met; (3) only one worker is present at night; and (4) retrofitting should be minimized. All options restrict the nighttime operating area to a space that one observer can see. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Equipment or an independent controller enforces speed and force limits, a person can stop operations immediately, and loss of connection triggers a safe stop. The model only proposes plans.
Model-calculated limits are passed to the existing controller, a person can stop operations immediately, and connection loss triggers a safe stop. The model proposes plans and limits.
Independent limits and an immediate manual stop are provided, but the robot completes its last plan after losing connection. The model proposes plans.
Independent limits and a safe stop on connection loss are provided, but there is no immediate human stop; the system relies on automatic stopping.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:A}}**

The policy requires a qualified person to observe operations and be able to stop them at any time, limits to be enforced independently of the model, and the system to stop or remain in a safe state on intervention or loss of connection to Anthropic.

- {{option:A}} meets all three requirements. It accepts the cost of an independent controller and potentially lower throughput than model-selected limits, while narrowing the nighttime operating area to what one person can supervise.
- {{option:B}} reduces retrofitting but lets the model determine the limits, failing the independent-control requirement. It pursues constraints (1) and (4) at the expense of (2).
- {{option:C}} continues the last plan after disconnection instead of ensuring the required safe state.
- {{option:D}} removes the person's ability to stop the operation immediately and fails the observation-and-stop requirement.

This is a section of the new policy, absent from the September 15, 2025 version. Recheck the applicable requirements after the effective date.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective November 12, 2026) › High-risk physical actions](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)

questions.title: Whether an essay-coaching service may add ghostwriting

Retain feedback on structure and reasoning, but do not provide complete ghostwritten essays for submission.
Permit school submission as long as the essay is labeled AI-written.
Offer complete ghostwriting only to adults.

- {{option:A}} treats consent as an exception that the policy does not provide.
- {{option:B}} retains support for learning and excludes submission-ready ghostwriting, accepting that the proposed premium feature must be abandoned.
- {{option:C}} adds disclosure but does not change the function of producing a complete essay for submission.

questions.title: An AI plan to expand external-channel content within four weeks of launch
questions.prompt:
Nuri Appliances' marketing team uses Claude to draft product comparisons and wants to increase content within four weeks of launching a new water purifier. Apply Anthropic's policy effective November 12, 2026.

- Constraint 1: Avoid the policy's prohibited false-provenance and concealed-sponsorship practices.
- Constraint 2: Do not increase this quarter's total advertising expenditure.
- Constraint 3: Publish comparison content on channels outside the company's website within four weeks.

Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Create six AI-powered appliance-review sites, publish comparisons without disclosing their operator, and cross-link the sites to look like independent outlets. Have staff verify facts before publication.
Increase this quarter's advertising budget to buy space in external media with sponsorship disclosures. Publish staff-reviewed AI-drafted comparisons and negotiate the schedule with the outlets.
Have staff check AI drafts and publish them as company content on its website and official accounts. Send samples to external creators for their own reviews, conditional on sponsorship disclosure.
Have staff check AI drafts and publish them as company content on its website and official accounts. Defer expansion to external channels until next quarter after evaluating the response.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

Constraints 1 and 3 are decisive. The applicable policy prohibits fake personas, accounts, outlets or organizations, astroturfing, fake reviews, concealed sponsorship of content intended to influence opinions, networks of apparently independent sites concealing a common source, and flooding search engines or AI systems with content that misrepresents its source or independence. Clearly identified company content and disclosed sponsorship are not among those practices. Each plan is executable; the difference is which constraint it violates.

- {{option:A}} quickly expands external channels, but its network conceals the operator and impersonates independent media, violating constraint 1.
- {{option:B}} discloses sponsorship and secures external channels, but increasing advertising expenditure violates constraint 2.
- {{option:C}} identifies company content and sponsorship, satisfies constraint 1, and reaches external creator channels without an advertising-budget increase, satisfying constraints 2 and 3. Recruiting creators and requiring disclosure reduce speed of reach and message control; sample-product costs and staff review are additional tradeoffs.
- {{option:D}} meets policy and budget requirements but postpones external expansion, violating the four-week requirement in constraint 3.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective November 12, 2026) › Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)

questions.title: Scope and controls for personalizing overdue-payment notices
questions.prompt:
Dasom Debt Management wants AI to personalize notices to overdue customers. Its 20 agents have interaction histories containing vulnerability information such as bereavement and illness. Apply Anthropic's current September 15, 2025 policy.

- Constraint 1: Personalize notices for individual customers to support the recovery-rate KPI.
- Constraint 2: Do not exploit vulnerability through pressure or abusive collection.
- Constraint 3: The 20 agents have approximately 1,000 hours per month in total for review. There are about 60,000 notices per month (approximately 3,000 hours at three minutes each) and about 2,000 cases with vulnerability signals (approximately 670 hours at 20 minutes of direct contact each).
- Constraint 4: Controls must be rules that can be explained in an audit.

Which personalization scope and controls are most appropriate?

options.text: Input the full interaction history, including vulnerability information, and use the tone with the highest response rate for each customer. Evaluate effects afterward using recovery metrics and refine wording standards.
Do not personalize: send every customer the same notice, have agents respond only to incoming inquiries, and review recovery rates monthly.

Exclude vulnerability fields from model input and personalize around repayment options and schedules. Filter pressure language with rule-based checks before sending, and have agents contact cases with vulnerability signals directly.

Exclude vulnerability fields from model input, but require an agent to read and approve every notice before sending to check for pressure language. Apply the same process to cases with vulnerability signals.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

Constraints 2 and 3 are decisive. Anthropic's current policy prohibits abusive or harassing debt-collection practices and deceptive or abusive practices exploiting age, disability, or socioeconomic circumstances. OpenAI also prohibits exploiting people's vulnerabilities. The design should therefore exclude vulnerability information from input, check pressure language using rules, and route vulnerability-signal cases to people.

- {{option:A}} offers the strongest personalization, but may use vulnerability to pressure customers and violates constraint 2.
- {{option:B}} avoids the policy risk but abandons personalization and the KPI objective in constraint 1.
- {{option:C}} partly preserves the KPI through options-and-schedule personalization, meets the policy through input exclusions and pressure-language rules, and allocates human time only to vulnerability-signal cases, approximately 670 hours. Its tradeoffs are narrower personalization and the burden of direct contact for those cases.
- {{option:D}} meets the policy but review of every notice takes approximately 3,000 hours, exceeding the 20 agents' 1,000-hour monthly capacity and violating constraint 3.

The debt-collection wording in the policy effective November 12, 2026 was not checked for this question. Reassess whether the same design remains appropriate after that version takes effect.

questions.title: Review design for automated pass/fail notifications
questions.prompt: Which design best satisfies Requirement 1?
questions.context:
> **Company overview:** Hangyeol Competency Assessment Institute provides national-certification exam preparation and administers internal promotion exams. This exam season has 9,000 candidates: 3,000 take constructed-response questions and the other 6,000 take only multiple-choice questions. There are 12 examiners, with five days remaining until pass/fail announcements.
>
> **Existing environment:** The OpenAI API assists with constructed-response grading, and the Claude API powers the candidate-information chatbot. The institute must meet both OpenAI's Usage Policies and Anthropic's Usage Policy effective November 12, 2026.
>
> **Requirement 1:** Automate pass/fail notifications. Multiple-choice scores use an answer key and passing-threshold rules; AI proposes constructed-response scores against a rubric. A qualified person must be able to review and change results before finalization, and the announcement schedule should be met as far as possible.
>
> **Requirement 2:** Introduce AI for online proctoring. Candidate features are (1) one-to-one comparison of the ID photo and candidate's face before the exam, (2) scores for 'nervousness/suspected cheating' inferred from facial expressions and gaze during the exam, and (3) automated exam invalidation after suspicious video is flagged. Candidates are dispersed nationwide, and there are eight proctors. At registration, candidates can choose whether to consent and use an alternative path: a proctor's video identity check. The consent form states only the one-to-one matching purpose.
>
> **Reference information:** Registration-region distributions and previous-season pass-rate data are available.

options.text: Have examiners review only constructed-response scores near the passing threshold (about 600 candidates), finalize the remaining AI scores and notify candidates, and finalize multiple-choice results using answer-key rules.
Have AI propose both constructed-response and multiple-choice scores, then have the 12 examiners finalize all 9,000 results before notification.
Treat applying the passing-threshold table to AI constructed-response scores as a fixed-rule operation, finalize and notify without human review, and process multiple-choice results the same way.

Have examiners finalize AI score proposals for all 3,000 constructed-response candidates before notification, and finalize multiple-choice scores using the answer key and passing-threshold rules without AI.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:D}}**

Requirement 1 specifies that a qualified person must be able to review and change results before finalization; the distinction between 3,000 constructed-response candidates and 6,000 multiple-choice-only candidates also matters. The applicable policy requires a qualified person to meaningfully review and have authority to change recommendations in education and certification decisions. It excludes cases where a model merely applies fixed rules, formulas, or algorithms without judging an individual. OpenAI likewise prohibits automating high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas, including education, without human review. Constructed-response scores involve model judgment and require review; multiple-choice scoring here does not use a model.

- {{option:A}} reviews only a subset near the threshold, leaving other constructed-response decisions unreviewed before finalization.
- {{option:B}} unnecessarily adds multiple-choice results, which do not need model judgment, to the review workload, making completion by 12 examiners in five days infeasible.
- {{option:C}} misapplies the fixed-rule exclusion: assigning a constructed-response score is a model judgment about an individual.
- {{option:D}} reviews every constructed-response result and handles multiple-choice scoring without AI, reducing examiner workload. The tradeoffs are approximately 50 reviews per examiner per day and a tight schedule until the announcement.

The registration-region distribution and previous-season pass rates in the reference information are distractors. Disclosure requirements are not the issue in this question.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy (effective November 12, 2026) › High-risk Use Case Requirements](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) · [OpenAI Usage Policies › Empower people](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/)

questions.title: Correcting retention wording in a feedback-feature notice
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Retail's privacy team plans to state in a Claude API service notice: 'All conversations you submit are deleted after 30 days.' It must revise this to match Anthropic's Privacy Center explanation of commercial-product retention.

- Constraint 1: State the retention period accurately for each category.
- Constraint 2: Include all four categories: ordinary inputs/outputs, inputs/outputs flagged for policy violations, classification scores, and feedback data.
- Constraint 3: Use a concise, customer-readable table with one line per category.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: List ordinary inputs/outputs as within 30 days and flagged content as up to two years, one line each, then combine classification scores and feedback into one line saying 'Other data has separate retention periods'.
Include all four categories, but explain legal-retention exceptions, separate ZDR agreements, and customer-retained file services in three or four sentences for each category.
Use one line each: ordinary inputs/outputs within 30 days; flagged content up to two years; classification scores up to seven years; feedback data five years.
Write only one line saying ordinary inputs/outputs are deleted within 30 days, and link to the terms for all other periods.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

Constraints 1 and 2 are decisive. Anthropic's Privacy Center explains that ordinary API inputs and outputs are automatically deleted within 30 days of receipt or generation. Inputs and outputs flagged for policy violations may be retained for up to two years, trust-and-safety classification scores for up to seven years, and feedback data, including thumbs-up/down and bug reports, for five years. Thirty days does not apply to every category. None of the four options gives a false numerical period; they differ in compliance with the presentation requirements.

- {{option:A}} gives accurate periods where stated, but groups classification scores and feedback rather than separately covering all four categories, violating constraint 2.
- {{option:B}} covers all four but uses several sentences each, violating the concise one-line table requirement in constraint 3.
- {{option:C}} accurately gives all four periods in one line each and meets all three constraints. Its tradeoff is that exceptions such as legal retention need separate wording outside the table.

Haneul Pharmaceuticals' security team is adding Google Workspace tools for clinical-trial document analysis to its data-classification table. Use information rights management to block Drive source uploads to Notebook, then permit regulated data in Notebook only through direct pasting.

questions.title: Handling a former salesperson's request for conversation copies
questions.prompt:
A former salesperson requests copies of work conversations from ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise. The privacy team has these constraints:

- Constraint 1: The response deadline is only seven days.
- Constraint 2: Claude has only two Primary Owners, and only one is working this week.
- Constraint 3: The requester has left the organization and cannot access the account.
- Constraint 4: The response must accurately explain what the copy excludes.
- Constraint 5: Deliver only the requester's own conversations.

Which procedure best reflects the different platform routes? In every option, the ChatGPT workspace owner receives and handles the request.

Have a Claude Owner enable member self-export so the former employee can download it directly. Explain that uploaded file contents are excluded.

Have the available Claude Primary Owner run an organization export and download it before the link expires, then deliver the downloaded file unchanged. Explain that items deleted by users or retention settings before export are excluded.

Have the available Claude Primary Owner run an organization export and download it before the link expires, then extract and deliver only that user's conversations. Describe it only as a 'complete conversation copy'.

**Correct answer: {{option:A}}**

Constraints 3, 4 and 5 are decisive. OpenAI's help documentation says ChatGPT Business and Enterprise members cannot self-export and must contact the workspace owner. Only a Primary Owner can run a Claude Team or Enterprise organization-wide export, and its download link expires 24 hours after delivery. Items deleted by users or retention settings before export begins are excluded. Member self-export must be enabled by an Owner; it includes only the member's conversations and excludes uploaded file contents. Organization exports continue to include data of removed users.
